account: Erik Brynjolfsson of Stanford and Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond of MIT studied the staggered rollout of a generative AI chat assistant to the technical support agents of a Fortune 500 enterprise software company that sells business process software to small and medium-sized businesses in the United States. Most of the agents worked from offices in the Philippines, either for the firm or for outside contractors. An AI customer-service software company that the authors do not name built the tool on OpenAI's GPT models, and the tool suggested replies to agents in real time. A seven-week randomized pilot with 50 agents came first, and most agents gained access between November 2020 and February 2021. In the 2023 working paper, which covers about 3 million chats by 5,179 agents, the authors report that access raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average and by 34% for novice and low-skilled agents. The version that the Quarterly Journal of Economics published in 2025 covers 5,172 agents and reports a gain of 15% on average. Customers were more polite and asked less often to speak to a manager, and attrition among agents with less than six months of tenure fell by about 10 percentage points. The most experienced and highest-skilled agents saw small gains in speed and small declines in quality. The study covers one firm, and the authors write that the attrition results call for more caution than the productivity results. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab funded the work.
